title: Regular Preterite Endings
bigQuestion: How does one small ending, and sometimes one accent mark, tell a listener that something is already over?

story.title: Saturday Night at the Concert
story.kicker: Two friends retell a concert, and every verb they use points back to last Saturday.
paragraphs: On Monday morning, Daniela sat down next to her friend Marcos before first period. She could not stop smiling. "¿Qué hiciste el sábado?" (What did you do on Saturday?) Marcos asked. Daniela answered right away: "¡Fui a un concierto!" (I went to a concert!) Her cousin had bought tickets weeks before for a band from Chicago that sings in Spanish and English.

"Llegamos temprano" (We arrived early), she said. "Compré una camiseta y un refresco. Luego, la banda empezó a tocar." (I bought a T-shirt and a soda. Then the band started to play.) Every verb in her story pointed to finished moments: arriving, buying, starting. Marcos noticed that she never said compro (I buy); she said compré (I bought).

"¿Cantaste?" (Did you sing?) Marcos asked. "¡Sí! Canté todas las canciones. Mi prima bailó toda la noche." (Yes! I sang all the songs. My cousin danced all night.) Daniela explained that after the show they ate tacos near the venue. "Comimos tacos al pastor y volvimos a casa a la medianoche." (We ate tacos al pastor and went back home at midnight.)

Marcos laughed. "Yo no salí. Miré una película y dormí." (I didn't go out. I watched a movie and slept.) Two friends, two very different Saturdays, but the same tool carried both stories: the preterite, the Spanish past tense for actions that started and finished at a clear moment. In this chapter you will learn its regular endings, the accents that make them work, and the spelling changes hidden in the yo form.
story.think: Daniela used compré, canté and llegamos. What do these verbs have in common, and how would you tell a friend about your own last Saturday?

lessons.title: A Finished Action in the Past
lessons.mainIdea: The preterite tells about an action that happened and ended at a specific time in the past.
reading: Picture a friend asking what you did yesterday. You answer with actions that are done: you ate lunch, you studied, you called your grandmother. Spanish has a special tense for these finished actions, the *pretérito* (the preterite). A tense is a set of verb forms that shows time. The preterite answers the question "What happened?" with actions that have a clear start and end.

Compare two sentences. "Hablo con mi abuela" means I talk with my grandmother, now or usually. "Hablé con mi abuela anoche" means I talked with my grandmother last night, and the call is over. The stem habl- stays the same. Only the ending changes: -o for now, -é for a finished past. That single ending carries the whole idea of time.

The preterite is used for single events (Llegué a las ocho, I arrived at eight), for actions in a series (Entré, saludé y me senté, I came in, said hello and sat down), and for actions with a set length (Estudié dos horas, I studied for two hours). English speakers sometimes use "did" in questions, like "Did you study?" Spanish does not need an extra word: "¿Estudiaste?" already means Did you study?

words.d: the preterite — the Spanish past tense for completed actions with a clear beginning or end
to speak or talk — regular -ar verb; preterite yo form: hablé
to arrive — regular -ar verb; preterite: llegué, llegaste, llegó
to study — regular -ar verb; preterite: estudié, estudiaste, estudió

look.title: A Finished Evening
look.text: Yesterday: Llegué a casa a las cuatro. (I arrived home at four.) Estudié una hora. (I studied for an hour.) Hablé con mi abuela. (I talked with my grandmother.) Each action began, happened, and ended. None of them is still going on.
look.prompt: Name three things you did yesterday that had a clear end. Try saying one of them in Spanish with an -é ending.

check.q: Which sentence tells about a finished action in the past?
choices: Hablo con mi abuela los domingos.
Voy a hablar con mi abuela.
check.why: Hablé is the preterite yo form of hablar, and anoche (last night) sets a finished past moment.

check.q: What does "¿Estudiaste?" mean?
check.why: Estudiaste is the tú preterite form of estudiar, so it asks about a finished past action. Spanish needs no word for "did".

check.q: Which use fits the preterite best?
choices: An action that happens every day
An event that happened once and ended
check.why: The preterite is for completed actions with a clear start or end, like a single past event.

lessons.title: Time Words That Signal the Past
lessons.mainIdea: Words like ayer, anoche and la semana pasada are clues that a preterite verb is coming.
reading: When Marcos asked about Saturday, the word el sábado told Daniela to answer in the past. Spanish speakers use many time words like this. *ayer* means yesterday. *anoche* means last night. Anteayer means the day before yesterday. These words set the moment, and the preterite verb tells what happened at that moment.

Another group uses pasado or pasada, meaning last or past. The ending matches the noun: *la semana pasada* (last week) uses pasada because semana is feminine, while el año pasado (last year) and el mes pasado (last month) use pasado because año and mes are masculine. A common mistake is la semana pasado, which breaks gender agreement.

You can also count back with hace. "Hace dos días" means two days ago. "Visité a mi tía hace una semana" means I visited my aunt a week ago. Notice the word order: English puts ago at the end, but Spanish puts hace first, then the amount of time. Time words can start or end the sentence: "Ayer bailé" and "Bailé ayer" both mean I danced yesterday.

words.d: yesterday — often signals a preterite verb: Ayer trabajé (Yesterday I worked)
last night — Anoche miré una película (Last night I watched a movie)
last week — pasada agrees with the feminine noun semana
ago — hace tres días means three days ago; hace comes before the amount

look.title: Clues in a Text Message
look.text: Lucía texts her cousin: "Anoche cené con papá. Ayer compré zapatos. La semana pasada visité a la abuela. ¡Y hace un mes empecé mi trabajo nuevo!" (Last night I had dinner with Dad. Yesterday I bought shoes. Last week I visited Grandma. And a month ago I started my new job!)
look.prompt: Find each time word in Lucía's message. Which one would you use to talk about something you did seven days ago?

check.q: Choose the correct phrase for "last week."
check.why: Semana is feminine, so it takes la and the adjective pasada.

check.q: How do you say "two days ago" in Spanish?
check.why: Spanish puts hace before the amount of time: hace dos días.

check.q: What does "Anoche miré una película" mean?
choices: Last night I watched a movie.
Tonight I will watch a movie.
Every night I watch a movie.
Yesterday morning I watched a movie.
check.why: Anoche means last night, and miré is the preterite yo form of mirar (to watch).

lessons.title: Present or Preterite?
lessons.mainIdea: The ending of the verb, not the stem, tells you whether an action is happening now or already happened.
reading: Imagine you hear only one word from a conversation across the cafeteria: "Trabajó." Did someone work, or does someone work? The ending -ó with its accent tells you it is past: he or she worked. "Trabajo" without an accent would mean I work. Listening for endings is the key skill of this chapter.

Here is a side-by-side walk-through with *trabajar* (to work). Present: trabajo, trabajas, trabaja. Preterite: trabajé, trabajaste, trabajó. The stem trabaj- never changes. You drop -ar and add a new ending. Every preterite ending for yo and for él or ella in regular verbs carries a written accent, and that accent is stressed when you say it.

Time words help too. "Siempre trabajo los sábados" (I always work on Saturdays) is a habit, so it takes the present. "El sábado pasado trabajé seis horas" (Last Saturday I worked six hours) is one finished event, so it takes the preterite. When you write, look for a time word first, then choose the ending that matches it.

words.d: to work — present trabajo (I work), preterite trabajé (I worked)
the ending — the part of a verb added to the stem to show who and when
the stem — the part of the verb left after you drop -ar, -er or -ir, like trabaj-

look.title: Same Stem, Different Time
look.text:
Now: Trabajo en una tienda. (I work in a store.)
Past: Trabajé en una tienda el verano pasado. (I worked in a store last summer.)
Now: Ella trabaja mucho. (She works a lot.)
Past: Ella trabajó ayer. (She worked yesterday.)
look.prompt: Point to the ending that changes in each pair. Which pair uses an accent to mark the past?

check.q: Which verb form means "she worked"?
check.why: Trabajó, with -ó and an accent, is the él/ella preterite form of trabajar.

check.q: Which sentence needs the present tense, not the preterite?
check.why: Siempre (always) describes a habit, which takes the present tense.

check.q: In trabajé, what is the stem?
check.why: The stem is what remains after dropping -ar: trabaj-. The ending -é shows yo in the preterite.

lessons.title: The Six -ar Endings
lessons.mainIdea: Regular -ar verbs use -é, -aste, -ó, -amos, -asteis and -aron in the preterite.
reading: Daniela said "Canté todas las canciones" (I sang all the songs). Let's build the whole preterite of *cantar* (to sing). Drop -ar to get the stem cant-. Then add: yo canté, tú cantaste, él or ella or usted cantó, nosotros cantamos, vosotros cantasteis, ellos or ellas or ustedes cantaron.

Every regular -ar verb works the same way. Bailar (to dance): bailé, bailaste, bailó, bailamos, bailasteis, bailaron. *comprar* (to buy): compré, compraste, compró, compramos, comprasteis, compraron. If you know the six endings, you know hundreds of verbs, because most -ar verbs in Spanish are regular.

A frequent mistake is adding an extra -s to the tú form: "cantastes" instead of cantaste. You may hear cantastes in casual speech in some places, but standard written Spanish uses cantaste. Another mistake is mixing present and past: "Ellos cantan anoche" should be "Ellos cantaron anoche." The -aron ending marks ellos in the past.

words.d: to sing — canté, cantaste, cantó, cantamos, cantasteis, cantaron
to dance — Mi prima bailó toda la noche (My cousin danced all night)
to buy — Compré una camiseta (I bought a T-shirt)
to play an instrument; to touch — La banda tocó dos horas (The band played for two hours)

look.title: Building Cantar Step by Step
look.text:
cantar → drop -ar → cant-
yo cant + é = canté
tú cant + aste = cantaste
él/ella/usted cant + ó = cantó
nosotros cant + amos = cantamos
vosotros cant + asteis = cantasteis
ellos/ellas/ustedes cant + aron = cantaron
look.prompt: Use the same steps to build all six preterite forms of bailar. Which two forms need an accent?

check.q: Complete: Anoche ellos ___ en la fiesta. (bailar)
check.why: Ellos in the preterite takes -aron: bailaron.

check.q: Which is the standard tú preterite form of comprar?
check.why: The tú ending is -aste with no final -s: compraste.

check.q: What does "La banda tocó dos horas" mean?
choices: The band plays for two hours.
The band will play for two hours.
The band played for two hours.
The bands played for two hours.
check.why: Tocó is the él/ella preterite of tocar, and la banda is singular.

lessons.title: The Accent That Changes Meaning
lessons.mainIdea: Hablo means I speak, but habló means he or she spoke, so the written accent matters.
reading: Look at two words that seem almost the same: hablo and habló. In hablo, the stress falls on HA. In habló, the stress moves to the last syllable, LÓ, and the written *acento* (accent mark) shows that move. The first means I speak. The second means he, she or you (usted) spoke. One mark changes both the person and the time.

The same thing happens with the yo form. Hable, with no accent, is a command form (let him speak, or speak! to usted). Hablé, with the accent, means I spoke. So the accent on -é and -ó is not decoration. Leaving it off turns a past-tense sentence into a different sentence. Teachers mark this as a meaning error, not just a spelling error.

Practice by saying pairs aloud and stressing the final syllable in the preterite: compro and compró, estudio and estudió, llego and llegó. Heritage speakers often say these correctly without thinking but forget the accent when writing. A good habit is to check every yo and él form in the preterite before you turn in your work.

words.d: the accent mark — the written mark on é or ó that shows stress and can change meaning
the syllable — a beat in a word; ha-bló has two syllables and the stress is on the last one
he, she or you (usted) spoke — preterite of hablar; compare hablo (I speak)

look.title: Hear the Stress Move
look.text:
HA-blo → I speak (now)
ha-BLÓ → he or she spoke (past)
ES-tu-dio → I study
es-tu-DIÓ → she studied
LLE-go → I arrive
lle-GÓ → he arrived
look.prompt: Say each pair out loud and clap on the stressed syllable. Then write one sentence using llegó.

check.q: What does "Mi hermano habló con el maestro" mean?
choices: My brother speaks with the teacher.
I speak with my brother's teacher.
My brother will speak with the teacher.
My brother spoke with the teacher.
check.why: Habló, with the accent, is the él preterite form of hablar: he spoke.

check.q: Which word means "I studied"?
check.why: Estudié, with -é and an accent, is the yo preterite form. Estudio is I study, and estudió is he studied.

check.q: A student writes "Ayer ella llego tarde." What is wrong?
check.why: Without the accent, llego means I arrive. The past she arrived is llegó.

lessons.title: Nosotros: Same Form, Two Times
lessons.mainIdea: For -ar and -ir verbs, the nosotros form is the same in the present and the preterite, so context decides.
reading: Here is a surprise. "Hablamos" can mean we speak or we spoke. For -ar verbs, the nosotros form ends in -amos in both the present and the preterite. The form is identical, so Spanish speakers rely on context: the time words and the rest of the conversation.

"Hablamos todos los días" means we talk every day, a habit in the present. "Hablamos ayer" means we talked yesterday, a finished past action. The word ayer does all the work. The same is true for *caminar* (to walk): caminamos can mean we walk or we walked. Look for clues like ayer, anoche, el lunes pasado or hace una hora.

This is also true for -ir verbs: vivimos means we live or we lived. But -er verbs are different. In the present, we eat is comemos; in the preterite, we ate is comimos. So *comimos* can only be past. Daniela's line "Comimos tacos" had to be about Saturday night, even without a time word.

words.d: to walk — caminamos means we walk or we walked, depending on context
the context — the words and situation around a sentence that help show its meaning
we ate — preterite of comer; the present is comemos, so comimos can only be past

look.title: Which Time Is It?
look.text:
A: ¿Qué hacen ustedes los domingos? (What do you all do on Sundays?)
B: Caminamos en el parque. (We walk in the park.)
A: ¿Y el domingo pasado? (And last Sunday?)
B: Caminamos a la playa. (We walked to the beach.)
look.prompt: Caminamos appears twice with different meanings. What words in the dialogue tell you which time each one means?

check.q: In "Ayer caminamos al parque," what time does caminamos show?
check.why: Caminamos looks the same in present and preterite, but ayer (yesterday) makes it past.

check.q: Which nosotros form can ONLY be past?
check.why: For -er verbs the present is comemos and the preterite is comimos, so comimos is always past.

check.q: Choose the best translation: "Llegamos a las nueve anoche."
choices: We arrived at nine last night.
We arrive at nine every night.
We will arrive at nine tonight.
They arrived at nine last night.
check.why: Anoche (last night) makes llegamos past, and the -amos ending means we.

lessons.title: One Set of Endings for -er and -ir
lessons.mainIdea: Regular -er and -ir verbs share the preterite endings -í, -iste, -ió, -imos, -isteis and -ieron.
reading: After the concert, Daniela and her cousin ate tacos. Let's build *comer* (to eat) in the preterite. Drop -er to get com-. Add: yo comí, tú comiste, él or ella comió, nosotros comimos, vosotros comisteis, ellos comieron. Notice the i in every ending.

Now try *vivir* (to live). Drop -ir to get viv-. Add the very same endings: viví, viviste, vivió, vivimos, vivisteis, vivieron. In the preterite, -er and -ir verbs are twins. That is good news: you learn one set of endings and use it for both groups.

Watch the accents again. Comí and comió both carry a written accent, just like canté and cantó. A common mistake is using -ar endings on an -er verb, like "comé" or "comó." Those are not Spanish words. Another is writing "comieron" as "comeron"; the ellos ending is -ieron, with the i before the e.

words.d: to eat — comí, comiste, comió, comimos, comisteis, comieron
to live — viví, viviste, vivió, vivimos, vivisteis, vivieron
to drink — Bebí un refresco (I drank a soda)
to write — Ella escribió una carta (She wrote a letter)

look.title: Twins in the Past
look.text:
comer → com-: comí, comiste, comió, comimos, comisteis, comieron
vivir → viv-: viví, viviste, vivió, vivimos, vivisteis, vivieron
The endings after the stem are identical. Only the stem is different.
look.prompt: Build the six preterite forms of escribir. Which forms carry a written accent?

check.q: Complete: Anoche yo ___ tacos al pastor. (comer)
check.why: The yo preterite ending for -er verbs is -í: comí.

check.q: Which form means "they lived"?
check.why: The ellos preterite ending for -ir verbs is -ieron: vivieron.

check.q: What does "Ella escribió una carta a su abuelo" mean?
choices: She writes a letter to her grandfather.
She wrote a letter to her grandfather.
I wrote a letter to her grandfather.
She will write a letter to her grandfather.
check.why: Escribió is the ella preterite form of escribir: she wrote.

lessons.title: Salir, Volver and Aprender in Action
lessons.mainIdea: The same -er and -ir endings let you tell a whole evening: going out, learning, and coming back.
reading: Marcos said "Yo no salí" (I didn't go out). *salir* (to go out, to leave) is irregular in the present yo form (salgo), but in the preterite it is completely regular: salí, saliste, salió, salimos, salisteis, salieron. Don't let a present-tense irregular scare you; check the preterite on its own.

*volver* (to return) is a stem-changing verb in the present: vuelvo, vuelves. In the preterite, -er stem changes disappear. You say volví, volviste, volvió, volvimos, volvisteis, volvieron, with the o from the infinitive. A common error is "vuelví," which mixes the present stem with a past ending.

Put them together and you can tell a night out: "Salimos a las siete. Aprendimos un baile nuevo. Volvimos a casa a las once." (We went out at seven. We learned a new dance. We came back home at eleven.) *aprender* (to learn) follows the pattern too: aprendí, aprendiste, aprendió. Three verbs, one set of endings, one clear story.

words.d: to go out, to leave — preterite is regular: salí, saliste, salió
to return, come back — preterite has no stem change: volví, volvió, volvieron
to learn — aprendí, aprendiste, aprendió, aprendimos, aprendieron

look.title: Marcos Tells His Evening
look.text: No salí el sábado. Comí pizza con mi hermana. Aprendí a jugar un videojuego nuevo. Mi mamá volvió del trabajo a las diez y todos bebimos chocolate caliente. (I didn't go out on Saturday. I ate pizza with my sister. I learned to play a new video game. My mom came back from work at ten and we all drank hot chocolate.)
look.prompt: List every preterite verb in Marcos's evening and give its infinitive.

check.q: Choose the correct form: Mi papá ___ a casa tarde. (volver)
check.why: -er verbs lose their stem change in the preterite, so the form is volvió.

check.q: Which is the yo preterite form of salir?
check.why: Salir is irregular only in the present yo (salgo). Its preterite is regular: salí.

check.q: What does "Aprendimos un baile nuevo" mean?
choices: We learn new dances every day.
We will learn a new dance.
check.why: Aprendimos is the nosotros preterite of aprender. For -er verbs, -imos is only past (present is aprendemos).

lessons.title: Asking and Answering About the Past
lessons.mainIdea: To answer a tú question in the preterite, switch the -aste or -iste ending to the yo ending -é or -í.
reading: Conversations about the past bounce between tú and yo. Marcos asked "¿Cantaste?" and Daniela answered "Canté." The question uses -aste, and the answer switches to -é. With -er and -ir verbs, "¿Comiste?" (Did you eat?) becomes "Sí, comí" (Yes, I ate). This switch is the most common move in real conversations.

A classic mistake is answering with the same form you heard: "¿Escribiste la tarea?" "Sí, escribiste." That answer means Yes, you wrote. You need escribí. When a teacher uses usted, the ending is -ó or -ió: "¿Terminó usted?" means Did you finish? and still takes a yo answer: "Sí, terminé."

To say no, put *no* before the verb: "No, no comí" (No, I didn't eat). The first no answers the question; the second makes the verb negative. English needs didn't, but Spanish just uses no plus the preterite. Question words work the same way: "¿Dónde comiste?" (Where did you eat?) "Comí en Pilsen" (I ate in Pilsen).

words.d: to finish — ¿Terminaste? (Did you finish?) Sí, terminé (Yes, I finished)
no, not — placed before the verb to make it negative: No comí (I didn't eat)
where? — ¿Dónde comiste? (Where did you eat?)
the homework — ¿Escribiste la tarea? (Did you write the homework?)

look.title: A Quick Exchange
look.text:
Mamá: ¿Terminaste la tarea? (Did you finish the homework?)
Hijo: Sí, terminé. (Yes, I finished.)
Mamá: ¿Comiste? (Did you eat?)
Hijo: No, no comí. (No, I didn't eat.)
Mamá: ¿Y llamaste a tu tía? (And did you call your aunt?)
Hijo: Sí, la llamé. (Yes, I called her.)
look.prompt: Write the son's answers if he did eat but did not call his aunt.

check.q: "¿Escribiste la tarea?" Choose the correct yes answer.
check.why: A tú question gets a yo answer. The yo preterite of escribir is escribí.

check.q: How do you say "I didn't eat"?
check.why: No goes before the verb, and comí is the yo preterite: No comí.

check.q: Your teacher asks "¿Terminó usted el examen?" What is she asking?
check.why: With usted, the -ó form means you (formal). She is asking whether you finished.

sections.title: Spelling Changes in the Yo Form

lessons.title: -car Verbs: Busqué and Toqué
lessons.mainIdea: Verbs ending in -car change c to qu in the yo preterite to keep the hard k sound: busqué, toqué.
reading: Say *buscar* (to look for) and listen to the hard k sound in bus-CAR. When you add the yo ending -é, the letters c + é would sound like s in most of the Spanish-speaking world, and the word would sound wrong. To keep the k sound, Spanish writes qu instead: busqué (I looked for).

This change happens only in the yo form. The other forms keep the c because the ending starts with a or o: buscaste, buscó, buscamos, buscasteis, buscaron. The same rule applies to *tocar* (to play an instrument): toqué, tocaste, tocó. And to *sacar* (to take out, to get a grade): saqué una A (I got an A).

This is not an irregular verb. The sound follows the regular pattern; only the spelling adjusts. Students often write "buscé" or "tocé." Say those aloud with Latin American pronunciation and you hear bus-SÉ, not bus-KÉ. The spelling change keeps the word's sound the same across all six forms.

words.d: to look for — yo form busqué; others keep c: buscaste, buscó
to play an instrument — yo toqué la guitarra (I played the guitar)
to take out; to get a grade — saqué una A (I got an A)
to practice — practiqué (I practiced), practicó (she practiced)

look.title: Keeping the K Sound
look.text:
buscar: bus-CAR (k sound)
busc + é → buscé? That would sound like bus-SÉ.
Fix: c becomes qu → busqué (bus-KÉ)
busc + ó → buscó (already sounds like k, no change)
Same move: tocar → toqué, sacar → saqué, practicar → practiqué
look.prompt: Why does buscó keep the c but busqué does not? Explain it in your own words.

check.q: Choose the correct form: Ayer yo ___ la guitarra. (tocar)
check.why: In the yo preterite, -car verbs change c to qu before é: toqué.

check.q: Which form does NOT change c to qu?
check.why: Only the yo form changes. Buscaste keeps c because the ending starts with a.

check.q: Why does sacar become saqué in the yo form?
choices: To keep the hard k sound before e
Because sacar is an irregular verb
To show that the subject is plural
Because all yo forms use qu
check.why: The spelling changes to keep the k sound; c before e would sound like s.

lessons.title: -gar and -zar Verbs: Llegué and Empecé
lessons.mainIdea: In the yo preterite, -gar verbs write gué and -zar verbs write cé: llegué, jugué, empecé, almorcé.
reading: Daniela said "Llegamos temprano," but if she were alone she would say "Llegué temprano" (I arrived early). *llegar* has a hard g sound. Before e, the letter g alone sounds like the Spanish j (a breathy h sound), so Spanish adds a silent u: llegué. The other forms stay plain: llegaste, llegó, llegaron. Jugar (to play a sport or game) works the same: jugué, jugaste, jugó. Pagar gives pagué.

Verbs ending in -zar change z to c before e. *empezar* (to begin) gives empecé (I began), but empezó (it began). *almorzar* (to eat lunch) gives almorcé. Here the sound does not change; Spanish spelling simply prefers ce over ze in most words, like cero and cena. Cruzar (to cross) gives crucé.

Put the three groups together with one memory line: car → qué, gar → gué, zar → cé, and only in yo. Other forms never change. A heritage speaker who says these words perfectly may still write "llegé" or "empezé" on a test. When you write the yo preterite of any verb ending in -car, -gar or -zar, stop and check the spelling.

words.d: to play a sport or game — jugué, jugaste, jugó; the u keeps the hard g
to begin, start — empecé (I began), empezó (it began)
to eat lunch — almorcé (I ate lunch), almorzaste, almorzó
to pay — pagué (I paid), pagó (he paid)

look.title: Example Receipt From the Concert
look.cite: Example prices made up for this lesson
look.prompt: Check the math: does 35 + 20 + 3 + 9 equal what Daniela paid? Then say in Spanish: I paid for the T-shirt (Pagué la camiseta).

check.q: Complete: Yo ___ al concierto a las siete. (llegar)
check.why: -gar verbs add u in the yo preterite to keep the hard g sound: llegué.

check.q: Which is the correct yo preterite of empezar?
check.why: -zar verbs change z to c before e, and there is no stem change in -ar preterites: empecé.

check.q: Which sentence is spelled correctly?
check.why: Jugó is the él form and needs no spelling change. The yo form would be jugué.

review.q: Which ending shows nosotros in the preterite of an -er verb?
review.why: -er and -ir verbs share -imos in the preterite: comimos, bebimos.

review.q: What does "Compraron boletos la semana pasada" mean?
review.why: -aron is the ellos/ellas/ustedes preterite ending, and la semana pasada means last week.

review.q: Choose the correct form: Anoche tú ___ muy bien. (cantar)
review.why: The standard tú preterite ending for -ar verbs is -aste: cantaste.

review.q: Which pair shows the spelling change correctly?
review.why: -gar verbs add u before é in the yo form: pagué.

review.q: Which sentence uses the preterite correctly?
choices: Ayer mi mamá trabajó ocho horas.
review.why: Ayer marks a finished past day, and trabajó is the ella preterite form.

review.q: Why is "Mi papá hablo con la maestra ayer" a mistake?
choices: Hablo means I speak; the past he spoke is habló.
Ayer cannot go at the end.
review.why: The accent moves the stress and changes the meaning: habló is he spoke.

review.q: Choose the correct form: Mi hermana ___ del trabajo a las seis. (volver)
review.why: -er stem changes do not happen in the preterite, and ella takes -ió: volvió.

review.q: Which yo preterite form is spelled correctly?
review.why: Sacar changes c to qu before é: saqué. The others should be practiqué, almorcé and empecé.
